title: Toilet Paper: Over or Under? The Answer Is Not in the Patent
parts: People say an eighteen ninety-one patent settles the toilet paper war.
The drawing shows the paper hanging over the roll.
Case closed, people say.
So we read the patent. All of it.
Not one word about how to mount the roll.
By the end, you will know which famous proof is a myth.
Over or under: you have a side. Let us see if you have evidence.
Today we sort every claim into four boxes.
Documented. Disputed. Myth. And no evidence found.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, the patent.
Seth Wheeler lived in Albany, New York. He ran a company that made perforated paper.
Nearly one hundred patents in his life.
On December twenty-second, eighteen ninety-one, he was granted one called Toilet-Paper Roll.
This is the document that went around. Its drawing shows a roll, with one sheet hanging from the top.
The drawing is documented.
But look at what is not there: no wall, no holder.
And the text never says how to mount a roll. Not once.
It is about perforations. Wheeler complains that sheets do not separate with certainty.
His fix: an angled cut, so each sheet tears off cleanly.
The curved cut, he adds, helps you find the end of a sheet.
That is what he patented. Not the direction.
He was fixing torn sheets, not settling your family argument.
Wheeler had patented rolls and wall holders years before.
So the eighteen ninety-one patent improved the roll. It did not start it.
Another patent that September shows a roll on a holder, with the sheet in front, from the top.
Its text says earlier holders were complicated and little used. It says nothing about direction.
A holder from eighteen ninety shows the roll beside a wall. The paper falls on the side away from the wall.
That is three drawings, all with the paper over. In two other drawings, we could not tell.
Our reading: to sell a cut, he had to show a sheet. Which way it hung was probably incidental.
Nobody can know what Wheeler thought.
In twenty fifteen, a tweet about the patent made the news.
The drawing shows over: documented.
The patent proves over: myth.
Now, the earliest fight we could find in print.
July fifteenth, nineteen seventy-seven. Ann Landers was an American advice columnist.
A reader signs herself Paper Crazy. She has argued with her relatives.
She says the paper should come over the top. They all disagreed.
Landers answers: there is no right or wrong way. It is strictly a matter of personal preference.
Readers wrote back.
On September twenty-sixth, she revisits the letter. She says she almost did not print it.
It seemed so inconsequential, she wrote.
Letters came, she says, from the four corners, including Samoa, Guadalajara, Athens, and Mexico City.
So much for inconsequential.
And her own choice? She sided with the sister-in-law, who wanted under.
Landers's reason? Her own mother did it that way.
So in nineteen seventy-seven, the columnist chose under. Not over.
You may have heard that she got fifteen thousand letters. That number is famous.
We traced it. It leads to a speech from nineteen eighty-six, reported second-hand.
We found no column, and no original of the speech.
Fifteen thousand letters: no evidence found.
Our reading: Landers treated it as taste, not science.
Her words, and her choice: documented.
So who prefers what? Here is the best number we found.
February twenty-second, twenty twenty-two. The polling firm YouGov asked nearly twenty-eight thousand American adults.
The question was simple: over or under?
Over: fifty-nine percent. Under: fourteen percent.
No preference: twenty-one percent. Not sure: six percent.
Our calculation: more than four to one. Of those who chose, about four in five pick over.
So in the United States, over wins: documented.
But only in the United States. We did not find a survey with a clear method for any other country.
Now another famous number.
In March twenty ten, the toilet paper brand Cottonelle issued a press release.
It said seventy-two percent of the votes in its own poll were for over.
The same release launched a new product. Its name: Roll Over. Subtle.
Those were votes on the brand's own website.
We could not check how it was run.
Our reading: a company's number is not an independent measurement.
Disputed.
Even so, a majority tells us what people do. Not why.
Now the reasons. People give five main ones.
Reason one: it is easier to find the end. Over, people say, keeps the loose sheet in view.
Our reading: plausible.
The only thing we found about that is Wheeler's cut, and it is not about direction.
Disputed.
Reason two: hygiene.
The idea: hang it under, and your hand brushes the wall. Hang it over, and it does not.
Our reading: that makes sense on paper. Pun intended. But we found no published test of it.
Disputed.
Reason three: children and pets. Under, people say, is harder to unroll.
In nineteen seventy-seven, a reader with two cats and two dogs wrote the opposite.
Same worry. Opposite advice.
Disputed.
Reason four: physics.
That same year, a reader signing as a physics professor said Landers's way needs less force.
Landers replied: I'll take your word for it.
In twenty sixteen, physicist Brian Wecht told Vice it does not matter. The forces are mirror images, he says.
Our reading: the roll may be symmetric. The wall and your hand are not.
Two opinions. No measurements.
Disputed.
Reason five: looks. Fancy paper with a design, one reader said, shows its pattern if it hangs over.
Another reader used the same pattern to defend under.
Same pattern. Opposite sides.
Disputed.
Our reading: that is what a habit looks like when it hunts for reasons.
Now the so-called studies.
Study one: Colorado. You may see a Colorado university study cited.
We could not find where that comes from. The closest real paper we found is this one.
It was published in November twenty eleven. Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder sampled twelve public restrooms.
Ten surfaces each, from toilet seats to soap dispensers.
We found no mention of toilet paper in it. Good science. Wrong question.
Our reading: a real paper can sound like proof, even when it studied something else.
As proof of over: no evidence found.
Study two: a blog. In February two thousand five, a blogger wrote that over wastes less paper.
It was a joke post, with diagrams.
It reports no measurement.
Five years later, an agency's web page called it an independent study.
A joke became a study.
As a study: myth. As a joke: fine.
So did the toilet paper makers ever set a rule?
We looked for a manual, or an advertisement, from the big brands. We found none that fixes a direction.
Old Scott ads talk about softness and purity, not direction.
A company rule: no evidence found.
Now, hotels.
In nineteen seventy-seven, a maid who had worked in several hotels wrote to Landers.
In several hotels, she said, staff are taught to hang rolls over. Why? She wrote: don't ask me.
That is one letter, not a rule.
Our reading: hotels repeat a habit. They do not explain it.
So could anyone settle this? Yes, with a simple test.
Our reading: many people, both directions, and count.
Count sheets per pull. Count torn perforations. Count how often a hand touches the wall.
We found no published test like it.
So here is the scoreboard.
The patent drawing shows over: documented.
The patent proves over: myth.
In nineteen seventy-seven, Landers called it personal preference, and chose under: documented.
Fifteen thousand letters: no evidence found.
Most Americans prefer over, in twenty twenty-two: documented.
The brand's own poll: disputed.
Colorado as proof: no evidence found.
The paper-saving study: myth.
The five reasons: disputed.
A company rule: no evidence found.
So is over better? We cannot say that. Nobody has shown it.
Is under better? Same answer.
Our reading: this is a custom. Many of us hang the roll the way somebody once hung it for us.
In nineteen seventy-seven, Landers did exactly that.
That does not make over wrong. It makes it a choice.
The answer was never in the patent. Our reading: it was in the bathroom where you grew up.
So the honest verdict: disputed. The famous proof is a myth.
Tell us in the comments: over or under, and what is your reason?
If nobody ever measured a reason, why does a backwards roll bother us so much?
And what other habit have you never checked?
